title: Building a crypto market intelligence engine with AI-assisted coding — looking for honest technical feedback
author: Vishalkool166
selftext:
I've been building a personal crypto market intelligence project called Crypto Engine, using AI-assisted coding to help develop and iterate on the system.

The project explores market analysis, trading-signal evaluation, and a dashboard. It's been a learning experience in application development, strategy logic, and the challenges of building something that needs to be tested properly.

To be clear, I haven't independently validated that the system is profitable, and I'm not presenting it as a proven trading strategy.

I'd appreciate constructive feedback, especially on the architecture, backtesting reliability, risk controls, and what you'd test before trusting a system like this.

GitHub: https://github.com/vishalkool166/crypto-engine

I'm the person building the project, and I'm happy to answer questions about the development process. Thanks!

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the honest test for a signal engine is logging every signal with a timestamp before the outcome exists and scoring them a month later. anything scored after the fact drifts toward looking good, mostly without you meaning it to.

replies.author: Vishalkool166
replies.body:
That's a good point. The system has signal tracking and outcome synchronization, but I want to verify that the full process genuinely captures signals before outcomes are known and evaluates them without hindsight bias.

That's exactly the kind of independent, end-to-end inspection I'm looking for—not just whether the bot runs, but whether its signals, backtesting, risk controls, and results can actually be trusted.

If you were reviewing the system, what would you inspect first to establish that?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the signal log itself. every row needs a write time stamped by the database, not by your code, and no row should change after it's written. if one was ever updated after its bar closed, the backtest has seen the future, whatever else checks out.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Saying plainly that it isn't validated is the right starting point. What I'd test first: that indicators match a trusted library on the same data, that signals use only closed candles (no look-ahead), and that the backtest includes fees, slippage and funding. Then an append-only signal log with timestamps, scored against a simple baseline over a held-out period, with the number of strategy variants you tried counted. For risk controls, hard limits (position size, daily loss, kill switch) should sit in code the signal logic can't change. Scheduled releases (CPI, FOMC) move crypto sharply, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for a no-trade filter around them.

replies.author: Vishalkool166
replies.body: Thanks for the detailed feedback. I used chatgpt to start auditing the system and identified gaps in backtest P&L, risk controls, and signal-log immutability. Your checklist is genuinely helpful.
